caption:
Why can't anyone unroll the Herculaneum scrolls?

In 1752, Bourbon workmen digging 120 feet down at Herculaneum hit a villa full of what looked like lumps of charcoal. Many were thrown away as exactly that. Then someone saw a faint trace of letters on one blackened mass.

They were papyrus scrolls, carbonised in an oxygen-starved room by the pyroclastic flows of Vesuvius in 79 AD. More than 1,800 rolls and fragments — the only library from antiquity that survives in its entirety.

Every attempt to open them destroyed something. Camillo Paderni sliced scrolls in half and copied what he could read, wrecking hundreds. Father Antonio Piaggio built a machine that pulled a roll open with silk threads; the first took four years, at millimetres per day, and the method destroyed the beginning of every papyrus it touched. Humphry Davy tried chlorine. The Louvre tried a small mill in 1877 and left a quarter of the scroll. An Oslo peeling method blew one roll into 300 pieces. And when a scroll did open, the ink faded on contact with air.

The carbon ink is chemically almost identical to the carbonised papyrus, so X-rays see nothing. What machines can see is thickness: ink makes the sheet very slightly thicker. In 2023 the Vesuvius Challenge paid a 21-year-old student $40,000 for the first word read inside an unopened scroll — porphyras, "purple." In June 2026 the team read one whole rolled scroll end to end: 22 columns, a Stoic treatise possibly by Chrysippus.

Still open: how much of the villa is unexcavated. A lower section of the collection may remain buried, and in 2016 academics warned the volcano could put it beyond reach.

Images: Herculaneum Papyrus 1521, British Library; an 1809 engraving of the unrolling apparatus; plates from Giacomo Castrucci's Tesoro letterario di Ercolano, Naples, 1858.
